pages.title: About
pages.content:
A small firm that walks the line

Brookmere, since 2009

Office

Where every plan is drawn

Slopes

GNSS on larger plots

Drafting

Hands, ruler, scale

Instrument

One hand on the focus knob

Since 2009

A firm opened in 2009

Ines Calloway opened Sokuten Survey in 2009 after twelve years with a county survey office. She wanted a smaller practice that still walked every line itself. The office and instrument room are at 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere. From there the firm takes house plots, garden boundaries, builders' setting-out and small land purchases within 40 km. Court disputes and estates over 2 ha sit outside that work, and the desk will name someone who does them. Ines remains the licensed land surveyor and signs every boundary plan. A visit still comes before any quoted survey: an hour on the ground, then a price that matches what was found.

Before any quote

One visit before a quote

A written price before anyone has stood on the plot tends to guess at pins, hedges and slopes. Sokuten Survey books the hour on the ground first. For 60 minutes Tomasz Reyes, the field lead, walks the line with you, looks for pins already in the ground, and sets the total station only after that walk. Felix Marlowe carries stakes, string and pin caps so anything found can be marked before you leave. Hana Sørli has already done the records and title research, so the hour starts with papers in hand. The $180 visit fee covers those 60 minutes, a field sketch and a written note. If you book a survey within 60 days, that fee is credited in full.

The plan

Drawn in the office, signed by Ines

After the visit, Amara Okonjo draws every measured plan from the field sketch, the instrument shots and the records prepared beforehand. Lukas Brandt adds GNSS and topographic work when the plot slopes or moves toward the larger sites the firm still accepts. A residential boundary survey covers up to 1,000 m², with pins found or reset, and leaves as a plan Ines Calloway signs. A topographic survey covers up to 2,000 m², with levels every 5 m and a plan with contours. The measured plan follows within 10 working days as a PDF and one paper copy. An extra folded A2 copy, posted, is $25. The plan records the line that was measured. It is not a substitute for work the firm does not take, including court disputes.

The field team

Ines, Tomasz, Amara and Lukas

Ines Calloway is founder and licensed land surveyor. She signs every boundary plan that leaves the office, and she set the practice up in 2009 so the person who signs has also stood on the kind of plot the firm accepts. Tomasz Reyes is field lead. The total station and the hour on the ground are his: the walk along the line, the shots of pins and corners, and the decision to bring the tripod out only once the line has been seen. Amara Okonjo handles plans and drafting. She draws every measured plan, so the paper matches the sketch you folded out on site. Lukas Brandt takes GNSS and topographic surveys, slopes and larger plots, including levels every 5 m up to 2,000 m².

The desk and the records

Priya, Felix and Hana

Priya Nandakumar keeps the client desk. She books every visit and answers the phone on +1 555 0142 090. A written request to visits@sokuten.example receives her reply within one working day. Felix Marlowe is field assistant. He sets the stakes, the string and the pin caps so the line stays visible after the hour ends. Hana Sørli does records and title research before each visit, which is why the first ten minutes at the gate are for reading deeds and any old plan, not for hunting papers. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30. Field visits run Monday to Saturday, with start times from 7:30 to 15:00. The firm is closed on Sundays and public holidays.

pages.title: The visit
pages.content:
The hour on the ground

60 minutes, 5 stages, 1 plan

Gate

0–10 min at the gate

Marks

Stakes and string

Tape

Measured along the fence

Pin

The pin you came for

60

minutes on site

5

stages

1

plan

Stage 1 · At the gate

0–10 min

The first ten minutes stay at the gate. You and the surveyor read the deeds and any old plan together, using the records and title research Hana Sørli prepared before anyone travelled. An old dimension, a neighbour's fence or a pin you have never seen gets named here, before the walk. If you have a copy, this is the moment it earns its place. If you do not, say so; the hour still starts from what Hana found and from what you know of the plot. Nothing is shot yet. The point of these ten minutes is to agree which line the visit is about, so the next stretch of time is spent looking for pins rather than guessing which boundary you meant.

Stage 2 · The walk

10–25 min

From ten minutes to twenty-five you walk the line with the owner. Tomasz Reyes leads that walk. The job is to look for the pins already in the ground: in turf, at a hedge corner, beside a fence, sometimes at the edge of a drive. You set the pace. Corners you care about, a stretch a neighbour has recently fenced, a slope where a house might sit, all belong on this loop. Felix Marlowe walks with the stakes and string but does not mark yet, because marking comes after the pins and corners have been seen. Most of the hour is this kind of walking. The instrument stays packed until the line is clear to the people who will live with it.

Stage 3 · The tripod

25–40 min

Minutes twenty-five to forty are the instrument's turn. The tripod goes down and the total station shoots the pins and the corners agreed on the walk. This is one concentrated spell, not a morning of measuring for its own sake. Lukas Brandt's GNSS work is a different booking, used for slopes and larger plots; a standard hour on a house plot or garden line stays with the total station. You can stand where you can see the shots without crossing the line of sight. What is shot is what was found and what you pointed out. If a pin is missing and an existing record shows where it should be, that fact is written down for a later pin reset rather than invented on the spot.

Stage 4 · The marks

40–50 min

From forty to fifty minutes the line is marked with stakes, string and caps you can see. Felix Marlowe sets them. The marks show what was found: pins that were already there, corners that were shot, and any gap where a pin was not in the ground. They are there so you, and a builder if you have one, can look along the same line after the team has gone. String on pale soil and caps on the pins are the visible record of the hour. They are not the measured plan. They are the reason the plan, when it arrives, should match something you have already stood next to and recognised.

Stage 5 · The sketch

50–60 min

The last ten minutes are at the field sketch. It is folded out and you agree what, if anything, comes next. That may be nothing more than the written note of the hour. It may be a residential boundary survey, a pin reset, setting-out for a builder, or a topographic survey. The sketch and the note are part of the $180 visit. No further work is booked on the plot unless you ask for it. The five stages are then finished: read, walk, shoot, mark, agree. You keep the sense of the line. The office keeps the measurements that Amara Okonjo will draw if a plan is what you decided you need.

Before you come

What to have ready at the gate

Have the address of the plot, any deeds, and any old plan if you have one. Two dates that suit you are enough when you first write. You do not need to prepare a speech; the first ten minutes are for reading those papers together. If a pin might sit under a driveway, a hedge or turf, say so, and make sure that edge can be reached during the walk. Wear what you would wear to walk your own boundary. The visit starts between 7:30 and 15:00, Monday to Saturday. Priya Nandakumar confirms the start when she replies. Office hours for that call or email are Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30, on +1 555 0142 090 or visits@sokuten.example.

Afterwards

After the visit

You leave with three things from the day itself only if they were part of the hour: the field sketch, the written note, and the marks on the ground. Stakes, string and caps stay so the line remains visible. The measured plan is the later piece. It follows within 10 working days as a PDF and one paper copy. Ines Calloway signs a boundary plan. Amara Okonjo draws it. An extra paper copy, folded A2 and posted, is $25. If you book the survey within 60 days of the visit, the $180 fee is credited in full against that survey. The invoice for the plan is sent after the plan, and it is due in 14 days.

Weather

If it rains

The hour depends on seeing the line, the pins and the marks. If rain hides the ground or makes the walk unsafe, the visit moves rather than forcing a shot you cannot check with your own eyes. Email visits@sokuten.example or call +1 555 0142 090 and Priya Nandakumar will offer another start between 7:30 and 15:00, Monday to Saturday. The five stages do not change on the new day. Reading at the gate still comes first. The tripod still comes out only after the walk. Sundays and public holidays stay closed. The fee for the hour remains $180, credited in full if a survey is booked within 60 days.

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
Fees

Six prices, written down

Published prices

All figures are in USD. A site visit, the hour on the ground, is $180. It covers 60 minutes on site, a field sketch and a written note. A boundary survey of a residential plot is $1,250. It covers up to 1,000 m², pins found or reset, and a signed plan. A pin reset is $160 per pin, for one missing pin where an existing record already describes it. Setting-out for a builder is $720. It covers the house footprint, one visit, and stakes and offsets. A topographic survey is $1,650. It covers up to 2,000 m², levels every 5 m, and a plan with contours. An extra paper copy of a plan is $25, folded A2 and posted.

The $180 visit fee is credited in full if a survey is booked within 60 days. The office is open Mon–Fri 8:30–17:30. Field visits run Mon–Sat, with start times from 7:30 to 15:00. Travel beyond 40 km is quoted before booking. The office is closed on Sundays and public holidays.

The visit and the survey

What the visit and the boundary survey include

The $180 visit is the hour described in five stages: deeds and any old plan at the gate, a walk to look for pins, shots of pins and corners, marks with stakes, string and caps, and a field sketch where you agree what comes next. It is the right first booking for a house plot, a garden boundary, a builder who needs the line understood, or a small land purchase within 40 km of 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere. The boundary survey at $1,250 is the measured follow-on for a residential plot up to 1,000 m². Pins are found or reset. The plan is drawn by Amara Okonjo and signed by Ines Calloway, the licensed land surveyor. It is delivered within 10 working days as a PDF and one paper copy.

The smaller jobs

Pins, setting-out, contours and an extra copy

A pin reset at $160 is for one missing pin when a record of that pin already exists. Each such pin is priced on its own. The work uses that existing record; it is not a search without papers. Setting-out at $720 is for a builder who needs the house footprint marked: one visit, stakes and offsets, so the digger meets a line that has already been set. A topographic survey at $1,650 suits slopes and larger plots up to 2,000 m². Levels are taken every 5 m and the plan carries contours. Lukas Brandt leads the GNSS and topographic side of that work. If you need another paper copy after the one included with a measured plan, a folded A2 sent by post is $25.

Credit, travel, payment

Credit, travel and payment

The $180 visit fee is credited in full if a survey is booked within 60 days. Travel beyond 40 km of the office is quoted before booking. There is no fixed travel figure on this page, because the quote depends on the journey and is agreed before you commit. The firm does not take court disputes or estates over 2 ha. Payment for a measured plan is by invoice after the plan, due in 14 days. Office hours for questions about a figure are Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30. Visits themselves run Monday to Saturday, with start times from 7:30 to 15:00. Write to visits@sokuten.example or call +1 555 0142 090. Priya Nandakumar books the hour and answers the phone.

How the visit works

pages.title: FAQ
pages.content:
Questions before a visit

Ask us anything else by phone

Before you book

Ten answers before a visit

These cover the hour on the ground, the plan that follows and the fees. For anything else, Priya Nandakumar answers the phone on +1 555 0142 090, Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30.

Do I need to be there?

Yes. The hour on the ground is walked with the owner. From 10 to 25 minutes you walk the line together so pins, fences and corners are the ones you actually mean. The first ten minutes at the gate are shared too: deeds and any old plan are read side by side, not interpreted in your absence. A builder may attend a setting-out visit, and the person buying a small parcel should be the one who walks it. If you cannot be there, book a different start. Starts run Monday to Saturday between 7:30 and 15:00. Priya Nandakumar arranges that time. The firm does not spend the hour on an empty plot and guess which line you cared about.

What if it rains?

If rain hides pins or makes the boundary unsafe to walk, the visit moves to another start. Seeing the line is the point of the hour, and shots taken when the ground cannot be checked are not how Sokuten Survey works. Call +1 555 0142 090 or email visits@sokuten.example. Priya Nandakumar will offer another time between 7:30 and 15:00, Monday to Saturday. The office itself is open Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30, and is closed Sundays and public holidays. The rest of the visit stays in the same order: read at the gate, walk, shoot, mark with stakes, string and caps, then agree the field sketch. The visit fee stays $180.

Will you talk to my neighbour?

The visit is booked with you. If a neighbour is beside the fence while you walk the line, you may ask them to look at a pin or at the field sketch. That is a conversation on the plot, not a mediation and not a case. Sokuten Survey does not take court disputes. The written note and, if you book one, the signed plan describe what was measured. They are not an agreement between households and they are not a filing. Ines Calloway signs boundary plans as the licensed land surveyor. She does not represent either side in a dispute. If the work you need is a dispute, the desk will name someone who does that work.

Is the visit fee credited?

Yes. The site visit is $180 and covers 60 minutes on site, a field sketch and a written note. If you book a survey within 60 days, that $180 is credited in full against the survey. The surveys on the fee list are a residential boundary survey at $1,250 for up to 1,000 m², a pin reset at $160 per pin where a record already exists, setting-out for a builder at $720, and a topographic survey at $1,650 for up to 2,000 m² with levels every 5 m. The credit applies when the survey is booked in that 60-day window. An extra paper copy at $25 is a separate small item, not the survey itself.

How far do you travel?

Visits are taken within 40 km of the office at 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere. House plots, garden boundaries, builders' setting-out and small land purchases inside that distance are the work. Travel beyond 40 km is quoted before booking. There is no flat travel price, so you see the figure and accept it before the hour is reserved. Estates over 2 ha are outside the practice even when they sit nearby, as are court disputes. Priya Nandakumar can tell you from the address whether the plot is inside the 40 km and whether it is the kind of site the firm walks. She replies to a request within one working day.

What should I have ready at the gate?

Bring deeds if you have them, and any old plan. The first ten minutes are for reading those papers together, along with the records and title research Hana Sørli has done before the visit. Also send, when you book, the address and two dates that suit you. Mention if a pin may lie under turf, paving or a hedge, so the walk can reach that point. You do not need to mark the plot yourself before the team arrives. Stakes, string and pin caps are brought by Felix Marlowe and set late in the hour, after the pins and corners have been shot. Starts are between 7:30 and 15:00, Monday to Saturday.

When does the measured plan arrive?

The measured plan follows within 10 working days of the survey. You receive a PDF and one paper copy. Amara Okonjo draws every measured plan. Ines Calloway signs every boundary plan. A further paper copy, folded to A2 and posted, is $25 if you need one. The field sketch and the written note from a visit exist on the day of the hour; they are not the measured plan. Setting-out leaves stakes and offsets on the plot from that visit. A topographic plan includes contours and is based on levels every 5 m, up to 2,000 m². The invoice is sent after the plan and is due in 14 days.

Who will I meet?

Seven people work at Sokuten Survey, and you will not meet all of them on the plot. Priya Nandakumar books every visit and answers the phone. Hana Sørli completes records and title research before the visit. On the hour, Tomasz Reyes is the field lead, with the total station, and Felix Marlowe assists with stakes, string and pin caps. Lukas Brandt takes GNSS and topographic surveys, slopes and larger plots. Amara Okonjo draws the plan afterwards. Ines Calloway, founder and licensed land surveyor, signs every boundary plan. The office and instrument room are at 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere. The firm was opened in 2009.

Which sites do you take?

A visit suits a plot before you build, a boundary that two households might read differently, and land you are about to buy, when that land is a small purchase rather than a large estate. Setting-out for a builder marks a house footprint. Garden lines and house plots are everyday work. The firm does not take court disputes, and it does not take estates over 2 ha. If that is your situation, ask the desk and they will name someone who does it. Everything accepted sits within 40 km of Brookmere unless a longer journey has been quoted first. The first step is still the same hour: 60 minutes, five stages, one decision about a plan.

How do I request a visit?

Email visits@sokuten.example with the address, any deeds or old plan you already have, and two dates that suit you. A phone call works as well, on +1 555 0142 090, during office hours Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30. Priya Nandakumar replies within one working day. She confirms a start between 7:30 and 15:00, Monday to Saturday. The visit fee is $180, credited in full if you book a survey within 60 days. You do not need a form. Sundays and public holidays are closed, so choose dates inside the visit days. Say if the plot is near the edge of the 40 km so travel can be quoted before anything is booked.

pages.title: Request a visit
pages.content:
Request a visit

Two dates and an address are enough

What to send

What to send

Two dates and an address are enough to start. Send the plot address, any deeds or an old plan if you have one, and two dates that suit you, to visits@sokuten.example. Priya Nandakumar reads that message and replies within one working day. She books every visit and answers the phone if you prefer to call +1 555 0142 090. In her reply she confirms a start time between 7:30 and 15:00, on a Monday to Saturday. If the address sits beyond 40 km of 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere, she quotes travel before the booking is made. If the job is a court dispute or an estate over 2 ha, she will say so and name someone who takes that work.

What the hour will be

The booking is for 60 minutes on the ground, in five stages, aimed at one decision about a plan. You meet at the gate and read the papers. You walk the line and look for pins. The tripod comes out for pins and corners. Stakes, string and caps mark what was found. The field sketch is folded out and you agree what, if anything, comes next. The fee is $180, including the sketch and a written note. If a survey is booked within 60 days, the fee is credited in full. A measured plan, when one is commissioned, follows within 10 working days as a PDF and one paper copy, and is invoiced after the plan, due in 14 days.

The office

Office

Sokuten Survey keeps its office and instrument room at 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere.

Phone +1 555 0142 090.

Email visits@sokuten.example.

Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30.

Field visits run Monday to Saturday, with start times from 7:30 to 15:00.

The office is closed on Sundays and public holidays.

The area for ordinary bookings is within 40 km of that address.

House plots, garden boundaries, builders' setting-out and small land purchases are the sites Priya books. Write in the subject that it is a visit request, and include the two dates in the message so the reply can offer a real start rather than a general note.

pages.title: The spring list
pages.content:
The spring list

Early dates before the calendar opens

Why it fills

Why spring and autumn fill first

Spring and autumn fill first because that is when people want a line marked before other work starts. A builder books setting-out so the house footprint, stakes and offsets are in place before excavation. An owner books a boundary while pins can still be looked for in grass, ahead of a fence. Someone about to buy a small parcel wants the hour on the ground while access to the plot still stands. Families dividing a garden often need both a topographic survey and a new boundary while the ground is open. The diary does not grow to match that rush. Visits run Monday to Saturday only, with starts between 7:30 and 15:00, and each one is a single hour led by Tomasz Reyes. Those two seasons simply ask for more of the same hours, so they fill before the quieter months do.

Two emails a year

What joining means

Joining the spring list means two emails and no others. One is sent in February. One is sent in August. Both come from visits@sokuten.example. They offer early dates before the calendar opens for the season ahead. They do not confirm a visit, do not hold a plot, and do not change a fee. The six prices stay as published: $180 for the hour, $1,250 for a residential boundary survey up to 1,000 m², $160 per pin reset where a record exists, $720 for setting-out, $1,650 for a topographic survey up to 2,000 m², and $25 for an extra folded A2 copy. A real booking is still a separate message with your address, any papers you have, and two dates. There is no other mail from the list.

How to join

How to join

Email visits@sokuten.example with the subject line Spring list and the address you are likely to need surveyed. Priya Nandakumar keeps the client desk and adds you for the February note and the August note. She still replies within one working day if you are actually requesting a visit rather than only joining the list. Say which you want, so an early-date note is not mistaken for a booking. Office hours for a reply are Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30. The phone is +1 555 0142 090 if you would rather ask how the two emails work. Travel, if the plot is beyond 40 km of 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere, is quoted only when you book, not when you join the list.

Join the spring list

The day itself

What happens next

On the day, plan for 60 minutes at the plot. The first ten are at the gate with the deeds and any old plan. Then you walk the line, the tripod comes out for pins and corners, Felix Marlowe marks what was found with stakes, string and caps, and the field sketch is agreed before anyone leaves. The visit is $180. If you later book a survey within 60 days, that amount is credited in full. A measured plan, if you commission one, follows within 10 working days as a PDF and one paper copy. Ines Calloway signs a boundary plan. The invoice is sent after the plan and is due in 14 days. Until Priya's reply arrives, you do not need to send the same request again.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Privacy

What we keep, and for how long

What you send us

Sokuten Survey is an independent land surveying firm at 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere. When you request a visit you send an address, any deeds or old plan you choose to include, two dates, and whatever name and contact details you put in the message. That material is used to book the hour, to prepare records and title research, and to draw and send a plan if you commission one. Phone calls to +1 555 0142 090 are taken by Priya Nandakumar for the same purpose. Email to visits@sokuten.example is the written route. We do not ask you to create an account. A measured plan is returned to you as a PDF and one paper copy. An extra posted copy goes to the address you give for that posting.

The spring list

If you join the spring list, we keep the email address you wrote from and use it for two messages only. One is sent in February. One is sent in August. Both concern early dates before the calendar opens. There is no other mail attached to the list. The list is not a booking, and the address of a plot is used only if you included it so we know which area the dates refer to. You can leave the list by writing to visits@sokuten.example and asking to be removed. Priya Nandakumar handles that request from the client desk. Office hours for a reply are Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30. Joining or leaving the list does not change the published fees.

Who sees the papers

Visit papers are used inside the firm by the people who do the work. Hana Sørli uses them for records and title research before the visit. Tomasz Reyes and Felix Marlowe use what they need on the hour. Lukas Brandt uses them for GNSS and topographic surveys. Amara Okonjo uses the field record to draw the plan. Ines Calloway uses it when she signs a boundary plan. Priya Nandakumar uses your contact details to reply and to book. We do not sell the contents of a deed, a plan or an email. A quote for travel beyond 40 km is prepared only so you can decide whether to book. Invoices are sent after a plan and relate to the fee you were shown.

How long we keep a file

We keep the correspondence, the field sketch, the written note and the measured plan for as long as the visit and that plan still need to be understood: a later extra copy, a pin reset from an existing record, or a question about what was signed. The $180 credit, if you book a survey within 60 days, depends on knowing the date of the visit, so that record is kept at least through that window. We do not keep a spring-list address after you have asked to be removed. To ask what we hold about you, or to correct an address or an email, write to visits@sokuten.example or call +1 555 0142 090. This page describes our own practice. It does not name outside advertisers, because the firm does not use them.

pages.title: Terms
pages.content:
Terms

The work, the fees and the plan

The work we accept

Sokuten Survey, of 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere, provides land surveying for house plots, garden boundaries, builders' setting-out and small land purchases within 40 km of the office. Travel farther than that is quoted before booking and proceeds only if you accept the quote. The firm does not take court disputes and does not take estates over 2 ha. If a request falls into either of those, we decline and will name someone who does that work. A booking is for the service you asked for, at the published USD price or at a travel quote given in advance. Founded in 2009, the firm is led by Ines Calloway, licensed land surveyor, who signs every boundary plan.

Visits, plans and marks

A site visit lasts 60 minutes and includes a field sketch and a written note. The five stages are reading at the gate, walking the line, shooting pins and corners, marking with stakes, string and caps, and agreeing what comes next. Field visits start Monday to Saturday between 7:30 and 15:00. You need to be present. A measured plan, when commissioned, follows within 10 working days as a PDF and one paper copy. A boundary plan is signed by Ines Calloway and drawn by Amara Okonjo. Stakes and caps left on the plot show what was found that day. They are a field mark, not the signed plan. The plan records the survey. It is not a decision in a dispute and not an undertaking about what a neighbour will do.

Fees and invoices

The site visit is $180. A boundary survey for a residential plot up to 1,000 m² is $1,250, including pins found or reset and a signed plan. A pin reset is $160 per pin where an existing record covers that pin. Setting-out for a builder is $720, for the house footprint, one visit, and stakes and offsets. A topographic survey up to 2,000 m² is $1,650, with levels every 5 m and a plan with contours. An extra paper copy, folded A2 and posted, is $25. The $180 visit fee is credited in full if a survey is booked within 60 days. Invoices for a plan are sent after the plan and are due in 14 days. Prices are USD on every version of this site.

Booking, rain and the spring list

Send a request to visits@sokuten.example or call +1 555 0142 090 in office hours, Monday to Friday, 8:30–17:30. Include the address, any deeds or old plan you have, and two dates. Priya Nandakumar replies within one working day. The office is closed Sundays and public holidays. If rain hides the line or makes the walk unsafe, the start is moved to another time inside the usual visit hours. The spring list is optional. It sends one email in February and one in August about early dates, and no other mail. Joining it does not reserve an hour and does not alter these terms. Asking to be removed ends those two emails. Questions about a booking go to the same address and phone.

categories.name: Field note
categories.description: What to have ready before the team arrives.

posts.title: The fence that sat 40 cm inside the line
posts.excerpt: Corinne Abara asked Sokuten Survey to walk a garden line after a neighbour's new fence went in, and two old pins turned up under the turf.
posts.content:
Corinne Abara asked for an hour on the ground because a neighbour's new fence had gone up along the garden and she was no longer sure the posts followed the boundary. She did not want a dispute prepared. She wanted the pins, if they were still there, found and the line marked where she could see it. Sokuten Survey booked the visit at her plot, within the ordinary round of house plots and garden boundaries the firm takes from its office at 14 Ferrow Lane, Brookmere.

Before anyone travelled, Hana Sørli did the records and title research that precedes every visit. The deeds and an older plan were the papers that mattered. They described a line the new fence might or might not have followed. That reading is the reason the first ten minutes of the hour happen at the gate, with the owner, rather than at a desk after the fact. Corinne brought what she had. The rest was already in the file.

From ten minutes to twenty-five they walked the line. The new fence was obvious. The pins were not. Garden turf had closed over the two old marks, and nothing in the fence itself announced where the recorded boundary sat. The walk was slow on purpose. Most of an hour at Sokuten Survey is spent this way. Tomasz Reyes, the field lead, looks for pins already in the ground before the total station leaves its case. Felix Marlowe walks with stakes, string and pin caps and does not set them until the shots are done.

The two pins were found under the turf. Once they were clear, the tripod went down. The stage between twenty-five and forty minutes is the only one given to the instrument: shoot the pins and the corners that the walk has already agreed. With those shots, the relationship to the new fence could be stated plainly. The fence sat 40 cm inside the line. That was the measurement of this visit. It was not a guess read off the posts, and it was not a figure carried in from another job.

Between forty and fifty minutes the found pins and the line were marked with stakes, string and caps. The marks were there so Corinne could stand at the garden and see the same thing the note would describe. A fence can look decisive simply because it is new. Caps and string are quieter, and they are easier to check against the pins than a memory of where a post seemed to be. The neighbour was not booked as a client. The hour had been booked with the owner who asked for it. What the marks showed was the measured line, not a settlement between the two households.

The last ten minutes were the field sketch, folded out on site. This is where the visit either stops or turns into a survey. Corinne and the surveyor agreed that a signed boundary plan should follow. The sketch and the written note were part of the $180 visit. The residential boundary survey was the next piece of work: a plot within 1,000 m², pins found or reset, plan drawn by Amara Okonjo and signed by Ines Calloway, the licensed land surveyor who signs every boundary plan the firm issues. Because the survey was booked from that visit, the $180 fee was credited in full, as it is whenever a survey is booked within 60 days.

The measured plan followed within 10 working days, as a PDF and one paper copy. It recorded the pins found under the turf and the fence 40 cm inside the line. It did not instruct the neighbour to move anything. Sokuten Survey does not take court disputes, and a plan is not one. Corinne had the paper she could show, the marks she could see, and a number that came from the pins rather than from the fence. If a further folded A2 copy had been needed, it would have been $25 posted. She had the copy the survey includes.

The useful order was the ordinary one. Read the deeds at the gate. Walk until the old pins show themselves. Shoot only then. Mark what was found. Agree the next step while the sketch is still in hand. The fence had looked like the boundary because it was built. The pins had been there longer, 40 cm away, under the turf.

posts.title: What to have ready at the gate
posts.excerpt: Deeds, an old plan and two minutes of walking shoes: what the first ten minutes need.
posts.content:
The first ten minutes of the hour are spent at the gate reading papers. Bring the deeds if you have them, and any old plan, even a sketch. Hana Sørli will already have pulled the record.

Wear shoes you can walk a line in. The middle of the hour is a walk, and turf, flower beds and the edge of a driveway often hide a pin.

If you know where you think the corners are, say so at the gate. Nothing is shot until the walk is finished.

posts.title: A footprint on a slope
posts.excerpt: Merrow & Daughters Build asked for setting-out on a 1-in-8 slope before the digger came.
posts.content:
Merrow & Daughters Build had a house footprint to place on a 1-in-8 slope and a digger booked for the following week. Rhea Merrow asked for setting-out, which is one visit, stakes and offsets, at $720.

Tomasz Reyes set the tripod once the line had been walked. Felix Marlowe drove the stakes and pulled the string for each corner, and every offset was marked so the crew could check the line without a second visit.

The crew set out from the stakes the same week. Nothing about the visit is special to a slope: the hour on the ground has the same five stages, and the published price for a builder is the same $720 within 40 km of Ferrow Lane.

posts.title: One garden, two houses
posts.excerpt: The Adeyemi family divided a long garden for two houses, with a topographic survey and a new boundary.
posts.content:
The Adeyemi family had a long garden and a plan to give half of it to a second house. Before anything could be drawn, the ground had to be known: its levels, its slope and where the old boundary ran.

Lukas Brandt took the topographic survey, up to 2,000 m² with levels every 5 m, and Amara Okonjo drew the plan with contours. Ines Calloway signed the new boundary after the pins were set.

The visit came first. The $180 fee for the hour on the ground was credited in full when the survey was booked inside 60 days.

posts.title: The pin under the driveway
posts.excerpt: A pin reset from a 1987 record, found 30 cm below new paving.
posts.content:
A 1987 record named a pin at the corner of a driveway that had since been repaved. Hana Sørli found the record before the visit, and Tomasz Reyes measured from two other pins that were still visible.

The old pin was 30 cm below the new paving. It was uncovered, checked and capped. A pin reset is $160 per pin when one missing pin has an existing record.

The cap now sits flush with the surface where anyone can see it.

posts.title: Why spring and autumn fill first
posts.excerpt: Dry ground, long light and builders ready to start: why those two seasons book early.
posts.content:
Spring and autumn are when the ground is dry enough to walk and the light is long enough for a full day in the field. They are also when builders and buyers want to move.

Field visits run Mon–Sat with start times from 7:30 to 15:00. Priya Nandakumar keeps a short early list for the first dates of each season, and the spring list page explains how to join it.

A visit is still $180, and it is credited in full if a survey is booked within 60 days.
